title: Tokens and names: make a calculation clear without changing it
goal: Identify the tokens in a statement, name quantities by their meaning, and check that renaming preserves behavior.

prerequisites.text: You can run an int main() scaffold and read std::cout from the previous lesson.
You know int name = value; and multiplication of small integers. No new types, functions, or loops are needed.

sections.title: What a, b and c stand for
paragraphs: A sensor takes 4 measurements, each lasting 250 milliseconds. The program calculates the total duration, but its author named the quantities a, b and c. Those names are enough for the machine; a reader has to recover their meaning.
Predict the output line. Then open the walkthrough: first identify the parts of the source, and then choose names that make the units clear to the next reader.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and follow the steps
paragraphs: Consider int count = 4;. Here int is a keyword, count is an identifier, = is an operator in the initializer syntax, 4 is an integer literal, and ; is a delimiter. Whitespace helps separate pieces but is usually not a language token itself. In count*4, the tokens remain distinct without spaces.

In std::cout << "duration_ms=" << count;, :: spans two characters but is one token; so does <<. A string literal may contain spaces: "total length" is not split into two identifiers. Header inclusion has special preprocessing rules; do not count the pieces of #include with a homemade whitespace splitter.
The value 1000 comes from 4 × 250, not from the names a, b and c. New names must preserve that relationship and the duration_ms= label.

sections.title: When whitespace changes meaning
paragraphs: int count=4; and int count = 4; declare the same object. But intcount = 4; no longer contains the int keyword: it contains a different name. Similarly, totalCount is one identifier while total Count is two. Inserting whitespace at an arbitrary position is not always formatting.

Indentation and line breaks outside literals help readability. Inside quotes, a space becomes output data: "length cm=" and "length_cm=" produce different strings. Therefore, formatting changes require a behavior comparison rather than visual inspection alone. Do not combine reformatting with a formula repair in one experiment.

sections.title: Choosing a valid name
paragraphs: Our examples use ASCII Latin letters, digits, and, when useful, underscores; a digit cannot come first. ASCII is a basic character set containing Latin letters and digits. sampleCount, count2, and period_ms follow our convention. A hyphen or space is not part of such a name: sample-count is parsed as names and subtraction.

This is a course convention, not a claim that C++20 forbids all non-Latin identifiers: specified additional characters are permitted. We restrict the alphabet for convenient typing and portability. Case matters: totalMs and totalMS are distinct names. Choose one style, such as lowerCamelCase, and use it consistently.

sections.title: Names already reserved by the language
paragraphs: int, return, const, and while have special language roles. You encountered while in Module 1; you do not need to write a loop here. A quantity cannot be named return. cout is not a keyword: it is a library name inside std. Editor coloring is a hint and does not replace compiler checks.

Some identifier-shaped forms are reserved for the implementation. Avoid double underscores anywhere and an underscore followed by an uppercase letter; our convention avoids any leading underscore. A compiler accepting a reserved name does not make its use valid: some reservation violations require no diagnostic. Thus a successful build is insufficient evidence of a good name.

sections.title: A name explains a quantity and its unit
paragraphs: a*b hides the meaning of a duration calculation. sampleCount * periodMs states that a sample count is multiplied by a period in milliseconds to obtain durationMs. The Ms suffix documents the unit. int does not distinguish milliseconds from centimeters; a unit error can compile successfully.

Do not encode an incidental current value in a name: samples4 becomes misleading when 4 changes to 6. Avoid restating the entire formula in an excessively long name. A useful name answers what the quantity means in the task. Internal durationMs and the external label duration_ms= may follow different conventions; renaming an object need not change the output contract.

sections.title: Rename one object at a time and compare
paragraphs: Record the original stdout first. Rename one declaration and all its uses, then build and compare output. Continue with the next name afterward. Text search helps, but blindly replacing a everywhere can corrupt main and labels. Match word boundaries and review every replacement.

Compare the original and renamed versions using identical data: the baseline first, then two more cases. Matching output confirms behavior for those cases; it is not a proof about every possible program. The table shows which names changed and which data stayed the same.

tables.caption: Names change; values and the label stay the same

sections.title: Intentional: a keyword used as a name
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
return has a grammatical role. Replace it with sampleCount everywhere.

sections.title: Intentional: a case mismatch
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
durationMs is declared; durationMS is a different name.

deep.title: Why can an identifier-shaped name still be reserved?
deep.text: Names containing a double underscore or beginning with an underscore followed by an uppercase letter are reserved for the implementation. A leading underscore is also reserved for names in the global namespace. The course therefore uses a simpler convention: do not start your own names with an underscore. This is our example convention, not the complete C++20 naming rule.

sections.title: Now solve a different problem
paragraphs: There are 5 panels, each 90 cm long. Rename a, b and c to panelCount, panelLengthCm and totalLengthCm. Preserve the values, formula and external length_cm= label. Then compare both versions for 0 × 90 and 2 × 140.
Open Practice. Its starter and your current source are separate from the worked examples. Write a prediction before running, then explain the result in your own words.

selfcheck.prompt: In the meaningfully named program, sampleCount is now 6 and periodMs is 125. The names and formula are unchanged. Which report results?
feedback: Correct: 6 × 125 = 750; the external label is unchanged.
1000 belongs to the earlier data, 4 × 250. A name does not fix a quantity to its old value.
durationMs is an internal name. The output string still begins with duration_ms=.

selfcheck.prompt: Which is one identifier following the course convention?
selfcheck.feedback: sampleCount starts with a letter and contains no minus operator.
A space inside a string literal belongs to its content.

selfcheck.prompt: The compiler accepted __cache. Is that sufficient to approve the name?
options: No: the form is reserved and a diagnostic is not required
Yes, if the value is small
selfcheck.feedback: Naming review supplements compiler checks. Compiler rejection is not a mandatory test expectation here.

selfcheck.prompt: Why is durationMs better than value4 in this calculation?
options: It describes role and unit rather than an incidental value
selfcheck.feedback: This helps a person; it is not a new type system and does not make an incorrect formula impossible.

practice.title: Naming review for a panel calculation
practice.task: There are 5 panels, each 90 cm long. Rename a, b and c to panelCount, panelLengthCm and totalLengthCm. Preserve the values, formula and external length_cm= label. Then compare both versions for 0 × 90 and 2 × 140.
criteria: All uses of each name agree; the names convey meaning and units and avoid reserved forms.
For each data set, output before and after renaming matches the corresponding result below.
Explain which tokens you replaced and which you preserved. Why does a successful build alone not verify the units?
practice.hint: Explain which tokens you replaced and which you preserved. Why does a successful build alone not verify the units?

steps.action: Map each of the three old names to its new name.
Rename one declaration and all its uses, build and compare output; repeat for the other names.
Check both versions for 5 × 90, 0 × 90 and 2 × 140. Do not change the formula while renaming.

terms.definition: A meaningful lexical unit such as a name, literal, or operator; not necessarily one character or a word separated by spaces.
A name form used in declarations and references to program entities.
A word with a special grammatical role, such as int or return; it cannot be declared as an ordinary quantity name.
A value written directly in source, such as 250 or "duration_ms=".
A team agreement about readable names that may be stricter than the language syntax.
A consistent name change in a declaration and all corresponding uses while preserving meaning.
